column2: Doyle’s text is given in his own words, complete, from the Harper printing of 1892. Where an older spelling would slow a reader or trip the voice, it has been brought up to date; nothing has been rewritten or abridged.
column3: Doyle’s text is given complete, from the Harper printing of 1892, and nothing is abridged. Where an older spelling or a word of his day would slow a reader or trip the voice, it has been brought up to date.

column2: The words are Doyle’s own. Where a word belonged to his day, or has changed its meaning since, it stays in the text, and a small lettered note at the end of the story says what it meant: a slavey was a maid-of-all-work.
column3: Where a word of Doyle’s day would puzzle a reader now, or has come to mean something else, a plain modern word stands in its place: a housemaid for his slavey, the barometer for “the glass,” handcuffs for “the bracelets.” Things that have no modern name, a hansom or a sovereign, keep the names he gave them. Where a speaker uses a foreign phrase, the English follows it. One word keeps a small lettered note: the carbuncle of The Blue Carbuncle is a gem.
